A classic dimensional-analysis problem: assume a power law and match the exponents.
**Step 1 — write the assumed relation.**
m = k v^a ρ^b g^c
with k a dimensionless constant.
**Step 2 — insert the dimensions.**
[M] = [L T⁻¹]^a [M L⁻³]^b [L T⁻²]^c
= M^b L^(a − 3b + c) T^(−a − 2c)
**Step 3 — equate the exponents on each side.**
M: **b = 1**
L: a − 3b + c = 0
T: −a − 2c = 0
**Step 4 — solve.** From the time equation, **a = −2c**. Substituting into the length
equation with b = 1:
−2c − 3 + c = 0
−c = 3
**c = −3**, hence **a = 6**
**Step 5 — assemble.**
m = k v⁶ ρ g⁻³
so
**m ∝ v⁶** ✓
**Why the dependence is so steep.** Doubling the river's speed multiplies the mass of the
largest movable stone by **2⁶ = 64** ✓ This is why a flood that runs only twice as fast
as a normal current can shift boulders it would otherwise leave untouched - and why
flash floods are so destructive.
**A check on the whole formula.**
[v⁶ ρ g⁻³] = [L⁶ T⁻⁶][M L⁻³][L⁻³ T⁶]
= M L⁰ T⁰
= **[M]** ✓ a mass, as required.
**The physical reason behind the sixth power.** A stone moves when the drag force, which
goes as ρv²d², overcomes its weight, which goes as ρ_stone g d³ ✓ Setting these equal
gives d ∝ v², and since m ∝ d³, it follows that m ∝ v⁶ - the same result from the
mechanics rather than the dimensions. This is known as **Airy's sixth-power law**.
**Reading the distractors.** **v⁴**, **v⁵** and **v** ✗ each fail the exponent equations:
only a = 6 satisfies both a = −2c and a − 3 + c = 0 together ✓
∴ v⁶.

Express G as a product of powers of c, g and p, and match the exponents.
**Step 1 — write down each dimension.**
c, speed of light: **[L T⁻¹]**
g, acceleration: **[L T⁻²]**
p, pressure, force per area: **[M L⁻¹ T⁻²]**
G, from F = Gm₁m₂/r²: **[M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²]**
**Step 2 — assume G = c^x g^y p^z and expand.**
[M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²] = [L T⁻¹]^x [L T⁻²]^y [M L⁻¹ T⁻²]^z
= M^z L^(x + y − z) T^(−x − 2y − 2z)
**Step 3 — equate exponents.**
M: **z = −1**
L: x + y − z = 3, so x + y = **2**
T: −x − 2y − 2z = −2, so x + 2y = **4**
**Step 4 — solve the last two together.** Subtracting:
y = 2, and then x = **0**
**Step 5 — assemble.**
**G = c⁰ g² p⁻¹** ✓
**Step 6 — verify.**
g²/p = [L² T⁻⁴]/[M L⁻¹ T⁻²]
= [M⁻¹ L³ T⁻²] ✓ exactly the dimensions of G.
**Why c drops out.** The exponent of c comes out zero, so the speed of light plays no
part ✓ That is not an accident of the algebra: g and p between them already supply all
three dimensions needed - p carries the mass, and g and p together fix length and time.
**The shortcut for this kind of question.** Start with the **mass** exponent, since
usually only one of the given quantities contains M ✓ Here p is the only one, so z = −1
immediately, and the rest follows from two simple equations.
**Reading the distractors.** **c⁰ g p⁻³** ✗ gives M⁻³, not M⁻¹. **c² g³ p⁻²** ✗ and
**c² g² p⁻²** ✗ both carry M⁻², and both leave c in, which the exponent equations
forbid ✓ Each can be eliminated in one line by checking the power of M alone.
∴ c⁰ g² p⁻¹.

Compute the area, then round to the significant figures the diameter justifies.
**Step 1 — find the radius.**
r = d/2
= 2·486/2
= **1·243 m**
**Step 2 — compute the area.**
A = πr²
= 3·142 x (1·243)²
= 3·142 x 1·545049
= **4·85454 m²**
**Step 3 — count significant figures.** The diameter 2·486 m has **four** ✓ and π is
given to four as well, so the product may carry no more than four.
**Step 4 — round.**
4·85454 → **4·854 m²** ✓
**Why four and not five.** The fifth digit would claim the diameter is known to better
than a millimetre, which the quoted 2·486 m does not support ✓ Rounding 4·85454 to four
figures gives 4·854, since the digit dropped is 5 followed by 4 - less than half.
**A check on the uncertainty.** If d = 2·486 ± 0·001 m, the relative error in d is
0·040%, and the area carries **twice** that, 0·080% ✓ On 4·854 m² that is **±0·004 m²**,
so the fourth significant figure is the last reliable one - exactly as the rule predicts.
**An alternative route.** A = πd²/4 = 3·142(6·180196)/4 = 19·4181/4 = **4·8545 m²** ✓ the
same value, confirming the arithmetic.
**Reading the distractors.** **4·85454 m²** ✗ keeps six figures, and **4·8545 m²** ✗
keeps five - both overstate the precision. **4·85 m²** ✗ keeps only three, discarding a
digit the measurement **does** justify ✓ Rounding too far is as much an error as not
rounding enough.
**A note on the printed units.** The options are labelled m³; an area is of course in
**m²**, and the exponent is a misprint. The numerical value is what the question tests.
∴ 4·854 m².

Find the screw-gauge least count, then combine the errors - remembering that the
diameter enters the density **cubed**.
**Step 1 — find the least count.**
LC = pitch/number of circular divisions
= 0·5/50
= **0·01 mm**
**Step 2 — find the measured diameter.**
d = main scale + (circular divisions x LC)
= 2·5 + 20(0·01)
= 2·5 + 0·20
= **2·70 mm**
**Step 3 — find the relative error in the diameter.** The uncertainty is one least
count:
Δd/d = 0·01/2·70
= 0·0037
= **0·37%**
**Step 4 — propagate to the density.** With
ρ = m/V = 6m/(πd³)
the relative errors combine as
Δρ/ρ = Δm/m + **3**(Δd/d)
= 2% + 3(0·37%)
= 2% + 1·11%
= **3·11%** ✓
**Why the factor of three.** The volume depends on the **cube** of the diameter, so the
relative error in d counts three times over ✓ Missing that factor gives 2·37%, and using
it incorrectly on the volume as a whole gives other wrong values - it is the heart of
this question.
**Why the errors add rather than combine in quadrature.** This is the **maximum possible
error** treatment used in school physics, in which the worst case is assumed ✓ A
statistical treatment would give √(2² + 1·11²) = 2·3%, but the options are built on the
simple sum.
**A check on the least count.** A pitch of 0·5 mm means the spindle advances 0·5 mm per
full turn, divided into 50 parts - so each division is **0·01 mm**, or 10 µm ✓ a typical
screw-gauge resolution.
**Reading the distractors.** **2·4%** ✗ adds only one power of the diameter error.
**0·9%** ✗ omits the mass error altogether. **4·2%** ✗ would need a diameter error of
about 0·73%, twice the actual ✓
∴ 3.11%.

A vernier reading is the main-scale value plus the vernier division number times the
least count.
**Step 1 — find the value of one main-scale division.**
1 MSD = **0·5 degree**
**Step 2 — find the least count.** Thirty vernier divisions match twenty-nine main-scale
divisions, so
LC = 1 MSD/number of vernier divisions
= 0·5/30
= **1/60 degree = 1 minute of arc**
**Step 3 — find the vernier contribution.**
9 divisions x (1/60)°
= 9/60
= **0·15°**
**Step 4 — add to the main-scale reading.**
58·5 + 0·15
= **58·65°** ✓
**Why the least count has that form.** Since 30 VSD = 29 MSD, one vernier division is
slightly **smaller** than a main-scale division:
1 VSD = (29/30) MSD
LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD = MSD(1 − 29/30) = **MSD/30** ✓
That small difference is what lets the vernier interpolate between main-scale marks.
**Reading it in minutes.** A least count of 1/60 degree is exactly **one arc-minute**, so
the reading is 58° 39′ ✓ Spectrometers are usually graduated to read half-degrees with a
vernier to the arc-minute, which matches this instrument exactly.
**A check on the magnitude of the correction.** Nine divisions out of thirty is less than
a third of one main-scale division, so the correction must be less than
0·5/3 = 0·167° ✓ The 0·15° found is just under that, as it should be.
**Reading the distractors.** **58·59°** ✗ uses 9/100 instead of 9/60. **58·77°** ✗
overshoots by more than one full main-scale division, impossible for a vernier reading.
**59°** ✗ rounds away the whole point of the vernier ✓
**The general rule.** reading = MSR + (VSR x LC), with LC = 1 MSD/N ✓ The same formula
serves callipers, screw gauges and spectrometers alike.
∴ 58·65°.

Find the mean and the mean deviation, then round the uncertainty against the instrument's
least count.
**Step 1 — compute the mean.**
(90 + 91 + 92 + 95)/4
= 368/4
= **92 s**
**Step 2 — compute each absolute deviation from the mean.**
|90 − 92| = **2**
|91 − 92| = **1**
|92 − 92| = **0**
|95 − 92| = **3**
**Step 3 — compute the mean absolute deviation.**
(2 + 1 + 0 + 3)/4
= 6/4
= **1·5 s**
**Step 4 — compare with the least count.** The clock reads to the nearest **1 s**, so no
quantity may be quoted to a finer precision than that ✓ The uncertainty 1·5 s must
therefore be rounded to a whole second, and it is rounded **up** - never down - so that
the error is not understated:
**Δt = 2 s**
**Step 5 — state the result.**
**(92 ± 2) s** ✓
**Why round the error up rather than to the nearest value.** Rounding 1·5 down to 1 would
claim a precision the data do not support ✓ The convention with uncertainties is always
to be conservative: an overstated error is honest, an understated one is not.
**Why the least count sets the floor.** No measurement from this clock can be better than
±1 s, so the reported uncertainty can never be smaller than that ✓ Here the scatter in
the readings is larger than the least count, so the scatter governs - but it must still
be expressed in whole seconds.
**A note on what is being measured.** Each reading is the time for **100 oscillations**,
so the period is 0·92 s ✓ Timing many swings at once is precisely how the 1 s least count
is beaten down to 0·01 s on the period - a standard laboratory technique.
**Reading the distractors.** **(92 ± 1·8) s** ✗ quotes the error to a tenth of a second,
finer than the clock can read. **(92 ± 5) s** ✗ takes the largest deviation rather than
the mean deviation. **(92 ± 3) s** ✗ likewise overstates it ✓
∴ (92 ± 2) s.
